title: When Humans Were Prey: Leopard Bites on an Ancient Jawbone
summary: Imagine being stalked by a leopard nearly 2 million years ago. That's what happened to an early human in Africa. A leopard sank its teeth into the person's face, leaving tiny marks on a jawbone. That bone, from a species called Homo habilis, tells a chilling story: humans were once prey. Homo habilis was one of the earliest members of our genus, which includes modern humans. Scientists found the jawbone at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, a famous site for ancient human fossils. At first, the marks looked like scratches. But a new study used artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze them. The AI compared thousands of tooth-mark images from modern carnivores. It found the marks were most likely made by a leopard. "That individual was preyed upon," said Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo, a study co-author. "Not scavenged." This matters because it changes how we picture early humans. For millions of years, our ape ancestors lived in trees and escaped danger by climbing. But by the time Homo habilis evolved, they walked upright and spent more time on the ground — where lions and leopards lived. To survive, they likely relied on each other, living in groups and sharing information about dangers. Over time, these behaviors may have helped humans become more cooperative. Today, we think of humans as top predators. But before we became hunters, we first had to survive being hunted.
why_it_matters: Knowing that our ancestors were once hunted, not hunters, helps explain why humans today are so good at working together and looking out for each other in our families and communities.

background_read: Homo habilis lived in East Africa roughly two million years ago; its name means "handy man" because it made simple stone tools, one of the first human species to do so.
Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania is one of the most famous fossil sites in the world, where the Leakey family and other scientists found many early human bones.
Big cats such as leopards and lions have lived in Africa alongside our early ancestors for millions of years, so being hunted was a real everyday danger.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists including Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo, studying a jawbone from an early human species called Homo habilis
WHAT: Marks on the jawbone were re-examined with artificial intelligence and turned out to be leopard bite marks, meaning the person was hunted
WHERE: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, a famous fossil site in Africa
WHY: It shows that early humans were prey before they became hunters, and that living in groups to share warnings may have helped our species survive

perspectives.description: They think AI gives scientists a powerful new way to read tiny clues on ancient bones that people might miss by eye.
They warn that tooth marks can look like other damage, so one bone is not proof that leopards regularly hunted early humans.
They see this as part of a normal food chain story: for millions of years our ancestors were prey like other animals, and only later became hunters.
